text.paragraph: Establishing primary care twelve days after discharge from a first psychiatric admission: provisional diagnosis and differential, antipsychotic monitoring baseline, missed periods, eating and exercise, and safety planning. list.item: First episode of psychosis with marked mood symptoms: about three weeks of little sleep, rapid speech, racing thoughts, grandiose plans and very long training days, then a voice commenting on her dancing and a belief that she was being watched and tested; tearful low mood since discharge. Diagnosis provisional; differential: bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type), and schizophreniform disorder or schizophrenia, depending on whether the psychosis ever occurred apart from the mood symptoms. Synthetic modern episode linked to her documented first hospitalization: resolved, provisional [S]

Bipolar I disorder, most recent episode manic with psychotic features, in full remission: the working diagnosis at three months, when her history, her journal, and her roommate's account (given with her consent) showed that the voice and the belief she was watched began only after weeks of manic symptoms and ended with them, with no psychosis since. Remains provisional: it would be revised to schizoaffective disorder if psychosis ever lasted two weeks or more without a mood episode. Synthetic modern episode linked to the documented breakdown and its retrospective interpretations: active, provisional [S]

Secondary amenorrhea: no periods for about four months before admission, during very heavy dance training at a low weight (BMI 18.7), with prolactin raised on risperidone; pregnancy test negative: resolved, confirmed [S]
Acute viral gastroenteritis (vomiting and watery diarrhea for two days, roommate with the same illness), with mild dehydration; resolved: resolved, confirmed [S]

Lithium level above the therapeutic range (1.4 mmol/L) during dehydration, with nausea and a worse fine tremor, without confusion or unsteadiness; lithium held and restarted; resolved: resolved, confirmed [S]

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Continue the antipsychotic started in hospital, with monitoring to the APA and ADA/APA standard: weight at every visit, blood pressure, fasting glucose or A1c and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks and yearly, prolactin because her periods have stopped, side-effect checks, and the AIMS at baseline and every six months

Psychiatry consultation with the first-episode psychosis coordinated specialty care team on the provisional diagnosis and how to settle it, a mood stabilizer to prevent another episode, and the antipsychotic choice given her raised prolactin and missed periods

Reproductive health on psychiatric medicines: a pregnancy test before any new medicine, valproate avoided because of its risks in pregnancy, counseling on the risks of any mood stabilizer in pregnancy, contraception that suits her, folic acid, and planning with psychiatry before any pregnancy

Eating and exercise: the SCOFF screen, menstrual and energy review at each visit, a sports dietitian, and a graded return to dance with food matched to the training load; training hours watched as an early warning sign

Coordinated specialty care: a care coordinator, individual therapy with psychoeducation about mood and psychosis, education for the people she chooses, support to return to dance and writing, and a peer specialist
Sleep and early warning signs: regular sleep and wake times, no all-night writing or training, and a plan to call the team after two short nights or if training hours climb

Lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily after a negative pregnancy test, with 12-hour trough levels 5 to 7 days after starting and after any change, then every 3 to 6 months (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L); creatinine and eGFR every 2 to 3 months for 6 months, then every 6 to 12; TSH once or twice in the first 6 months, then every 6 to 12; calcium yearly; and sick-day rules: hold it during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration, and avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers
Switch from risperidone to aripiprazole: aripiprazole 10 mg daily with risperidone 1 mg for one week, then risperidone stopped; prolactin and periods checked at three months
Structured safety assessment, a written safety plan with early warning signs, lethal-means counseling, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, the PHQ-9 at each visit, and safety review at every visit

Lithium sick-day plan, written down and shared with her roommate with her consent: stop lithium during vomiting, diarrhea, fever with poor drinking, or heavy sweating without fluids, and call the clinic; restart when eating and drinking normally; no anti-inflammatory painkillers; and go to the emergency department for confusion, unsteadiness, slurred speech, or a coarse tremor
No manic, depressive or psychotic episode and no readmission through six months
No episode and no admission; lithium and aripiprazole continued

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 2026-05-11: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with close follow-up. She has no thoughts of suicide or self-harm now and had none during the admission. Her risk is higher in the months after a first episode, and especially in a depressive phase after mania, so a written safety plan was made with her, with her own early warning signs (sleeping less, training for hours, racing thoughts, or feeling hopeless) and what to do about each. Lethal-means counseling: she has no firearm and no access to one; any medicine that is dangerous in overdose will be dispensed in small amounts while her mood is low. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was given and saved in her phone, with the clinic number. Safety reviewed at every visit [S]
